design_detail: Clinical narrative review for clinicians by four clinical pharmacists (University of Kansas School of Pharmacy; Harding University College of Pharmacy; UCSD Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences), updating the first, second and fourth authors' 2008 review in the same journal. The authors searched PubMed and Google Scholar for English-language literature from 1946 to 2016 with the keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative and abuse, plus individual drug names, added references cited in those papers, and kept publications on urine testing in humans or human samples; numbers of records and selection steps are not reported. The review covers screening immunoassays and confirmation (GC-MS, LC-MS/MS), federal workplace cutoffs (Table 1), approximate urine detection times (Table 2, adapted from the 2008 review), specimen validity, and by drug class the agents reported to give positive (true or false) or negative immunoassay results (Table 4, adapted from the 2008 review), with short sections on alcohol and tricyclic antidepressants. The section on specimen validity and adulteration was read but is not extracted, because the site does not give guidance on evading tests. No appraisal tool or synthesis. Read as the article-in-press version, whose pages (1-23) differ from the version of record.
can_establish: What these authors, from a non-systematic reading of the literature, list as federal workplace cutoffs, approximate urine detection windows, and medicines, foods and products reported to cause positive or negative immunoassay results by drug class, and their advice that screening results are presumptive and need GC-MS or LC-MS/MS confirmation before consequential decisions.
cannot_establish: How often a listed agent actually causes a false positive (frequencies are given for a few agents only, and Table 4 mixes true and false positives without naming assays or concentrations), how accurate the detection windows of Table 2 are (they come from textbooks, laboratory web pages and older reviews, without cutoffs, amounts or conditions), or whether listed interferences still apply to current assays.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: PubMed and Google Scholar, English, 1946 to 2016; keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative, abuse, and individual drug names; references cited in retrieved papers added; only publications on urine testing in humans or human samples kept (PDF pp. 1-2, Literature Search). No other criteria, counts or screening process are reported.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. The detection times in Table 2 come from nine sources (references 9-17): a 1987 report of a Council on Scientific Affairs in JAMA, a pain-medicine review, a textbook on the effects of psychoactive drugs, the authors' 2008 review, two laboratory web pages on synthetic cannabinoid testing, a psychiatry textbook chapter, Verstraete (2004) and an article in Pharmacist's Letter; Table 4 draws on case reports, package inserts and studies of specific older assays.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; the review summarizes how urine tests detect drugs and their metabolites.

comparison.controls: Not applicable; the reference standard for screening results throughout is confirmation by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS, as cited.

outcomes.instruments: Urine immunoassays (enzyme-multiplied immunoassay technique, ELISA, fluorescence polarization immunoassay; laboratory-based or point-of-care), GC-MS and LC-MS/MS confirmation, federal workplace cutoffs (PDF pp. 2-3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Point-of-care results are read visually and can be faint or uncertain (PDF p. 2); a result below the cutoff is reported negative, which does not mean the drug is absent (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Detection time: how long a drug can be detected in urine and still give a positive result (PDF p. 3). Table 4's 'potential positives' include true and false positives; 'potential medications that may not be detected' are false negatives.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, mostly lists and single figures (see key findings); no pooling or intervals.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection; frequencies of interference are given for only a few agents, sometimes without saying what they are percentages of; the assays behind most Table 4 entries are not named; the specimen-validity section is outside this card's extraction.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A non-systematic summary: federal cutoffs (Table 1), approximate urine detection times taken from secondary sources (Table 2), and agents reported to give positive (true or false) or negative immunoassay results (Table 4), with frequency data for a few. The review covers false negatives as well as false positives and qualifies weak evidence in the text (a single case report for proton pump inhibitors, one case series without confirmation for lamotrigine, no evidence for amoxicillin).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract promises an overview of false-positive and false-negative data and a useful tool for clinicians (PDF p. 1); the tables give lists rather than data on how often each interference occurs or with which assay, and the values in Table 2 carry no conditions. The highlights state "All positive results on immunoassays need confirmatory testing" (PDF p. 2), which is firmer than the text's advice to use clinical judgment on whether to confirm, with confirmation always before legal, employment and other consequential decisions (PDF p. 2). Otherwise the conclusions stay within the evidence.

timeline.event: Controlled poppy-seed study carded in this project (morphine and codeine in urine after eating poppy seeds), relevant to the review's poppy-seed statements but not cited by it
Narrative review of detection times in blood, urine and oral fluid, one of the nine sources of Table 2 (reference 16)
The first, second and fourth authors' earlier Mayo Clinic Proceedings review (Moeller, Lee & Kissack, 2008), from which Tables 2 and 4 are adapted; not read.
Monitored-abstinence study of urinary THCCOOH in 60 people who used cannabis regularly (last positive screen up to 29.8 days after admission), not cited by the review
Review of false-positive interferences with urine immunoassays from 2000 on, overlapping with this review's sources and disagreeing on the efavirenz result for the Drug Screen Multi 5 test (PDF p. 4)
Secondhand cannabis smoke study summarized by the review (PDF p. 8); the primary paper, carded in this project, had 18 non-smoking participants, 6 per session

replication.where_it_stands: A practical reference whose specific figures are second-hand. Its central advice (screens are presumptive; confirm by mass spectrometry before consequential decisions; know the laboratory's cutoffs and which drugs an assay cannot detect) agrees with Saitman et al. (2014); its detection times rest on older secondary sources and should be checked against primary studies such as Goodwin et al. (2008) for cannabis.

funding.funder: None stated in the article-in-press PDF read (no funding, grant or acknowledgment section).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article-in-press PDF read; whether the version of record adds one could not be checked (it is not among the files).
funding.affiliations_note: Clinical pharmacists in schools of pharmacy (PDF p. 1). Tables 2 and 4 are adapted, with permission, from three of the authors' own 2008 review in the same journal, and one cited study on oxycodone metabolites has the third author as co-author. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For detection windows: controlled-dosing and monitored-abstinence studies for each drug, at the cutoffs and with the assays used in practice, in people with typical patterns of use, reporting the full distribution of detection times. For false positives: systematic testing of current immunoassays against candidate medicines at concentrations found in patients' urine, with rates of unconfirmed positives by medicine in large confirmed datasets.

domains.note: Databases, years and keywords are stated, but not how records were selected or how many; Google Scholar searches cannot be reproduced; Table 2 rests on textbooks, laboratory web pages, a newsletter and older reviews.

No formal appraisal, but the text qualifies the evidence for several agents (one case report for proton pump inhibitors; one case series without confirmation for lamotrigine; no evidence for amoxicillin; NSAID interference rare); Table 4 lists all agents without the quality of evidence.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Tables 2 and 4, the review's core, are adapted from three of the authors' own 2008 review; no primary studies of the authors carry the conclusions.
Practice advice is marked as such and most factual statements carry citations; exceptions are listed under reporting issues.

domains.domain: Balance of reports of interference against evidence of no interference
domains.note: The text gives some negative evidence (amoxicillin, local anaesthetics, nabilone, ketamine in 3 patients, 93 medicines without cross-reaction on one synthetic cannabinoid assay) and covers false negatives, but Table 4 lists agents from single reports without noting negative findings, except for one footnote on the Vicks inhaler.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is careful in places and covers false negatives as well as false positives, but its selection is unsystematic, its detection-time table rests on secondary sources, and its interference table mixes true and false positives without assays, concentrations or frequencies. It may be cited for: the federal workplace cutoffs of Table 1 (as cited from the 2008 federal guidelines); the principle that screens are presumptive and that GC-MS or LC-MS/MS confirmation should precede legal, employment or other consequential decisions; approximate urine detection windows, labelled as approximate and second-hand; named examples of medicines, foods and products reported to cause positive screens, with the specific figure where one is given; and known false-negative gaps (opiate immunoassays and semisynthetic or synthetic opioids; benzodiazepine glucuronides and clonazepam; synthetic cannabinoids on cannabis tests). It may not be cited for how often a medicine causes a false positive, for an individual's detection time, or for the performance of current assays; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Search: PubMed and Google Scholar, English, 1946-2016, keywords urine drug test, screen, false-positive, false-negative, abuse and individual drug names, plus references cited in retrieved papers; only publications on urine testing in humans or human samples were kept; numbers of records and selection steps are not given.

Screening and confirmation: immunoassay screens, in the laboratory or at the point of care, are presumptive; GC-MS is the criterion standard for confirmation, identifying and quantifying the specific substance, and LC-MS/MS is an alternative; the authors advise always confirming before legal, forensic, academic, employment or other decisions with significant consequences, and their highlights say all positive immunoassay results need confirmatory testing.
key_findings.locator: Article Highlights; Methods of Drug Testing, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cutoffs: a result below the cutoff is reported as negative, which means the concentration was below the cutoff, not that the drug was absent; laboratories may use cutoffs different from federal ones; lower cutoffs reduce false negatives but may raise false positives; federal cutoffs were set for adults and for the workplace.
key_findings.locator: Methods of Drug Testing › Cutoff Levels, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Federal workplace cutoffs, screen and then confirmation (ng/mL): marijuana metabolites 50, THCCOOH 15; cocaine metabolites 150, benzoylecgonine 100; codeine/morphine 2000 and 2000; 6-acetylmorphine 10 and 10; phencyclidine 25 and 25; amphetamine/methamphetamine 500, then 250 each (methamphetamine confirmation also needs amphetamine of at least 100); MDMA 500, then MDMA, MDA and MDEA 250 each.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (from the 2008 federal mandatory guidelines, reference 7)

key_findings.finding: Detection time depends on the drug (half-life, metabolites, interactions, dosing interval, amount, chronic versus occasional use, time of last use) and on the person (body mass, urine pH, urine concentration, kidney or liver impairment).
key_findings.locator: Methods of Drug Testing › Detection Times, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Approximate urine detection times (Table 2): alcohol 7-12 hours; amphetamine and methamphetamine 48 hours; barbiturates, short-acting (pentobarbital) 24 hours, long-acting (phenobarbital) 3 weeks; benzodiazepines, short-acting (lorazepam) 3 days, long-acting (diazepam) 30 days; cocaine metabolites 2-4 days; marijuana, single use 3 days, moderate use (4 times a week) 5-7 days, chronic use (daily) 10-15 days, chronic heavy smoker more than 30 days; codeine 48 hours; heroin (as morphine) 48 hours; hydromorphone 2-4 days; methadone 3 days; morphine 48-72 hours; oxycodone 2-4 days; phencyclidine 8 days; synthetic cannabinoids, single use 72 hours, chronic use more than 72 hours; synthetic cathinones variable. Note: adapted from the authors' 2008 review; its nine sources (references 9-17) are mostly secondary; no cutoff, assay or amount is given for any value, and only marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids are split by pattern of use. [The table says 'chronic heavy smoker', not 'daily'; the note's 'no ... condition' overlooked the use-pattern rows.]
key_findings.note: Adapted from the authors' 2008 review; its nine sources (references 9-17) are mostly secondary, and no cutoff, assay, amount or condition is given for any value.

key_findings.finding: Cannabis testing: screening immunoassays detect several THC metabolites (federal cutoff 50 ng/mL; some laboratories may use a lower cutoff of 20 ng/mL), and GC-MS or LC-MS/MS confirmation is specific for THCCOOH at a federal cutoff of 15 ng/mL; detection depends on route, amount and potency, frequency of use, body mass and metabolic rate; with chronic use THC accumulates in fat and its metabolites are eliminated slowly, so urine detection can last more than 30 days after stopping in people who used chronically, whereas a single exposure in people who do not use cannabis is typically detectable for up to 72 hours. [Hedge restored: 'may use'.]
key_findings.locator: Specific Drugs Tested in the Urine › Cannabinoids, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, recent versus past use: glucuronides of THC and 11-OH-THC were studied as markers of use within the last 8 hours, but Lowe et al. found them (concentrations of these markers, by context) in urine up to 24 days after a person who used heavily stopped, which the review says refutes their usefulness; THC was detectable in blood after 30 days in 5 people (Bergamaschi et al.), and blood THC can fall quickly within the first hour. [The source does not say 'THC' was found in urine at 24 days.]

Prescribed cannabinoids: dronabinol (synthetic THC) tests positive for THC and cannot be told apart from plant THC by confirmation, while nabilone tests negative; a urine test for the plant cannabinoid THCV, meant to separate cannabis from dronabinol, was positive in only 50% of participants who used cannabis heavily (5 times per week, as printed) (Levin et al.). ['At least' is not in the source.]

Cannabis screens and medicines or products: proton pump inhibitors (evidence limited to one pantoprazole case report and its package insert), NSAIDs (Rollins et al.: 2 false positives in 510 samples, one with daily ibuprofen and one with chronic naproxen use; called rare) and efavirenz (well documented; its glucuronide metabolite) are reported to cross-react; several baby wash products, investigated because false-positive THC screens in newborns had increased, gave dose-dependent responses on THC immunoassays, many positive at a 20 ng/mL cutoff and none reaching 50 ng/mL. [The review does not say the responses were in newborns' urine.]

Secondhand cannabis smoke: 1980s studies mostly found urine metabolite levels well below standard cutoffs; THC potency of seized cannabis rose from about 3% in the 1980s to about 12% in 2014; in Cone et al., non-smokers spent 1 hour in a small room with people smoking cannabis of 5.3% or 11.3% THC with or without ventilation: with ventilation none screened positive at 20 ng/mL; without ventilation several were positive at 20 ng/mL and one at 50 ng/mL (11.3% THC), 2-22 hours after exposure, which the authors call harsh conditions a person would notice.
key_findings.note: The review describes 6 non-smokers exposed under three conditions; the primary study as carded in this project (sc_cone_2015) had 18 non-smoking participants, 6 per session, each in one session.

key_findings.finding: Opiate screens and false negatives: most opiate immunoassays are calibrated to morphine and cross-react little with oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone and oxymorphone; fentanyl, methadone and buprenorphine are not detected by morphine-specific immunoassays and need specific immunoassays or LC-MS/MS; some laboratories do not test for semisynthetic or synthetic opioids unless asked; Table 4 lists buprenorphine, fentanyl, meperidine, methadone, oxycodone, oxymorphone and tramadol as possibly not detected.
key_findings.locator: Central Nervous System Depressants › Opioids, 3rd paragraph (both columns; the right column of p. 9 starts without an indent and continues it); Table 4 (pp. 6-7)

key_findings.finding: Poppy seeds and heroin: the federal opiate cutoff was raised from 300 to 2000 ng/mL (morphine) in 1998 to limit positives from poppy seeds and prescribed opiates, and this high cutoff can miss recent opioid use; the heroin metabolite 6-acetylmorphine is specific to heroin but has a half-life of 36 minutes and is detected only up to 8 hours in urine; street heroin may contain acetylcodeine, making heroin, codeine and morphine use hard to tell apart.
key_findings.locator: Opioids, 4th and 8th paragraphs (the paragraphs are one lower than stated because the p. 9 right column continues the 3rd)

key_findings.finding: Opiate and methadone screens and medicines: ofloxacin was positive on the EMIT II opiate assay at a 300 ng/mL threshold while norfloxacin and ciprofloxacin were not (Meatherall & Dai); gatifloxacin gave a positive at 2000 ng/mL in a case report; rifampin has also caused false positives; verapamil, diphenhydramine and doxylamine have been reported to cause false-positive methadone screens; codeine can produce small amounts of hydrocodone, and hydrocodone of hydromorphone, which should not be read as use of those drugs when high concentrations of codeine or (as printed) hydromorphone are detected; hydromorphone is also a minor metabolite of morphine. Locator: Opioids, 5th, 7th and 10th paragraphs; Table 4 (pp. 6-7). [The 'reported' hedge and the condition were missing, and the paragraph numbers were one too high.]

Benzodiazepine screens and false negatives: most immunoassays target free oxazepam or nordiazepam, so benzodiazepines excreted as glucuronides (lorazepam, alprazolam) are missed without beta-glucuronidase hydrolysis, which most laboratories do not do; clonazepam (as 7-aminoclonazepam) cross-reacts poorly; 200-300 ng/mL cutoffs set for older benzodiazepines are often too high for potent ones; lowering the cutoff to 100 ng/mL with hydrolysis increased positives for alprazolam and triazolam, and 40 ng/mL was recommended for 7-aminoclonazepam; chronic diazepam use can be detectable for over 30 days, triazolam perhaps for a day.

Benzodiazepine screens and medicines: false positives are called minimal; sertraline is widely reported, with rates of 27% to 32% in two retrospective studies; oxaprozin and efavirenz also interfere, efavirenz only with the Triage 8 and Drug Screen Multi 5 tests.
key_findings.note: What the 27-32% are percentages of is not stated. Saitman et al. (2014, PDF p. 4) report the Drug Screen Multi 5 as negative on efavirenz presumptive positives in one of the studies cited here.

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine screens are the immunoassays most often linked to false positives; agents commonly linked are pseudoephedrine and ephedrine, bupropion, labetalol and ranitidine, with metformin, selegiline (metabolized to l-methamphetamine and l-amphetamine; metabolites found in hair up to 4 weeks after one dose) and the Vicks VapoInhaler also named; lisdexamfetamine is converted to d-amphetamine and is detected; in a Department of Defense analysis, the supplement ingredient DMAA was found in 92.3% of false-positive amphetamine samples that GC-MS confirmed negative.

Table 4 lists 33 agents (editors’ count) as potential positives (true or false) on amphetamine immunoassays: amantadine, aripiprazole, atomoxetine, benzphetamine, bupropion, chlorpromazine, clobenzorex, desipramine, dextroamphetamine, dimethylamylamine, ephedrine, fenproporex, isometheptene, isoxsuprine, labetalol, l-deprenyl, l-methamphetamine (Vicks inhaler; newer immunoassays no longer react), MDMA, metformin, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, phentermine, phenylephrine, phenylpropanolamine, promethazine, pseudoephedrine, ranitidine, ritodrine, selegiline, thioridazine, trazodone, trimethobenzamide and trimipramine.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, Amphetamines row and footnote b
key_findings.note: The table names no assays, concentrations or frequencies and mixes true positives (for example dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine, MDMA) with false positives.

key_findings.finding: Table 4, other screens: alcohol, short-chain alcohols such as isopropyl alcohol; benzodiazepines, efavirenz, oxaprozin, sertraline (may not detect alprazolam, clonazepam, lorazepam); cannabinoids, baby wash products, dronabinol, efavirenz, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors (may not detect nabilone, synthetic cannabinoids); cocaine, coca leaf tea and topical anaesthetics containing cocaine; opioids, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine and doxylamine (methadone assays only), heroin, opiates, poppy seeds, quinine, quinolones, rifampin, verapamil (methadone assays only); phencyclidine, dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, ibuprofen, imipramine, ketamine, lamotrigine, MDPV, meperidine, mesoridazine, thioridazine, tramadol, venlafaxine and O-desmethylvenlafaxine; tricyclic antidepressants, cyclobenzaprine and quetiapine, and carbamazepine, cyproheptadine, diphenhydramine and hydroxyzine (serum only, footnote f); synthetic cannabinoids, lamotrigine. [Footnote f is also on carbamazepine.]
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and footnotes e and f

key_findings.finding: Cocaine screens test for benzoylecgonine and have minimal cross-reactivity; the claim that amoxicillin causes false positives lacks evidence (Reisfield et al. found no false positives on 4 immunoassays); coca leaf teas, drinks and other products can make cocaine screens positive, and topical or ophthalmic cocaine can give true positives; benzocaine, lidocaine, procaine and tetracaine do not cause false positives. [Both statements are hedged with 'can' in the source.]

PCP screens: detection about 8 days; false positives reported with tramadol (case reports in overdose or misuse), dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, ketamine (one case report in a child sedated for imaging; in another report 3 people reporting recent ketamine use screened negative), venlafaxine (frequently, at standard doses and in overdose), lamotrigine (one case series of 2 patients without confirmatory testing) and MDPV (all spiked urine samples positive above 0.0031 mg/mL; mephedrone not); Rengarajan and Mullins reported false-positive PCP rates of 24% with dextromethorphan, 22% with tramadol and 15% with diphenhydramine in urines that GC-MS did not confirm.
key_findings.note: What the 24%, 22% and 15% are percentages of is not explained.

key_findings.finding: Synthetic cathinones: attempts to detect them in urine have not given good results; validation studies of one commercial immunoassay (Randox Drugs of Abuse V biochip) found mephedrone and MDPV concentrations below acceptance criteria with a high negative bias; parent cathinones are excreted rapidly in urine, with an elimination half-life of about 12 hours, and urine pH can influence the amount excreted. Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected by cannabis tests; little parent drug reaches urine; most assays target JWH-018 and JWH-073 metabolites; there is no accepted cutoff (assays 5-25 ng/mL); in Barnes et al., several of 73 synthetic cannabinoids cross-reacted, raising the cutoff from 5 to 10 µg/L increased false negatives by 12%, newer compounds (PB-22, RCS-4, RCS-8, XRL-11, AKB48) were poorly detected and none of 93 common medications and metabolites cross-reacted; laboratories estimate detection for 48 to 72 [hours] after last use. [The source does not say 'the only' assay validated; pH is said to affect the amount excreted, not the half-life.]
key_findings.locator: Designer Drugs and Herbal Drugs of Abuse › Synthetic Cathinones, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Synthetic Cannabinoids, 4th to 7th paragraphs; Table 4 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol: ethyl glucuronide (EtG) is the preferred urine marker because it is detectable for 2 to 5 days after drinking; incidental exposure from hand sanitizers or mouthwash can give positive results, and the ratio of EtG to ethyl sulfate may help tell drinking from incidental exposure.
key_findings.locator: Other Agents Tested in UDT › Alcohol, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Tricyclic antidepressant screens: carbamazepine, cyclobenzaprine and quetiapine commonly cause false positives; in one comparison with serum chromatography, 7 of 20 positive point-of-care urine screens matched therapeutic serum levels, 7 were subtherapeutic and 6 supratherapeutic or toxic; clomipramine was positive in only 50% of patients on the Syva Rapid Test and consistently negative on the Biosite Triage.

The authors conclude that results should be discussed with each patient, that decisions should involve a multidisciplinary team and the patient, and that clinicians should know their laboratory's cutoffs and work closely with laboratory directors.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 attributes the amphetamine-screen reaction of the Vicks inhaler to l-methamphetamine (p. 6), while the text says the inhalers contain 1% to 2.5% d-methamphetamine; the text then says neither isomer was detected in urine at a limit of 10 µg/L after 28 inhalations, yet that l-methamphetamine was present in most specimens at 11 hours at concentrations below 250 µg/L (p. 13).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which isomer the product contains and whether it was detected cannot be settled from the review; read Smith et al. (2014) before citing.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says efavirenz interference with benzodiazepine screens occurs only with the Triage 8 and Drug Screen Multi 5 tests, citing Blank et al. (2009) and Röder et al. (2007); Saitman et al. (2014, PDF p. 4) report the Drug Screen Multi 5 as negative on the efavirenz presumptive positives in Blank et al.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which point-of-care tests react to efavirenz is uncertain; read the primary papers before naming tests.

reporting_issues.issue: The secondhand-smoke study of Cone et al. (2015) is described as 6 non-smokers placed in a room under three conditions; the primary paper, as carded in this project (sc_cone_2015), had 18 non-smoking participants, 6 per session, each in one session.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the primary study for numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives single values without cutoff, assay or amount (only marijuana and synthetic cannabinoids are split by pattern of use), from mostly secondary sources (references 9-17); it also gives 48 hours for heroin (as morphine) but 48-72 hours for morphine, while the text gives 6-acetylmorphine only up to 8 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: The values are approximate and second-hand; they should not be presented as the detection time of a particular test.

reporting_issues.issue: Several frequencies are given without saying what they are proportions of: sertraline '27% to 32%' (p. 12) and the PCP false-positive 'rates' of 24%, 22% and 15% (p. 14).
reporting_issues.consequence: They cannot be read as the chance that a person taking the medicine will screen positive.

reporting_issues.issue: The highlights say all positive immunoassay results need confirmatory testing, while the text says clinicians should use clinical judgment to decide whether confirmation is necessary, with confirmation always for decisions with significant consequences.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the text's conditional advice is the authors' position.

reporting_issues.issue: Units are missing in places: laboratories estimate synthetic cannabinoid detection at '48 to 72 after last use' (p. 16; Table 2 gives 72 hours and more than 72 hours), and the methadone and EDDP assay cutoffs are given as 300 ng and 500 ng (p. 10).

disagreements.first_pass: Synthetic cathinones: the only commercial immunoassay validated (Randox biochip) measured mephedrone and MDPV below acceptance criteria with a high negative bias; cathinones are excreted in urine with an elimination half-life of about 12 hours, influenced by urine pH. disagreements.reviewer: Synthetic cathinones: attempts to detect them in urine have not given good results; validation studies of one commercial immunoassay (Randox Drugs of Abuse V biochip) found mephedrone and MDPV concentrations below acceptance criteria with a high negative bias; parent cathinones are excreted rapidly in urine, with an elimination half-life of about 12 hours, and urine pH can influence the amount excreted. Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected by cannabis tests; little parent drug reaches urine; most assays target JWH-018 and JWH-073 metabolites; there is no accepted cutoff (assays 5-25 ng/mL); in Barnes et al., several of 73 synthetic cannabinoids cross-reacted, raising the cutoff from 5 to 10 µg/L increased false negatives by 12%, newer compounds (PB-22, RCS-4, RCS-8, XRL-11, AKB48) were poorly detected and none of 93 common medications and metabolites cross-reacted; laboratories estimate detection for 48 to 72 [hours] after last use.
